summary: Specifies a Diameter application letting a Diameter server authenticate, authorize, and collect accounting data for Mobile IPv4 services. With the base protocol's inter-realm ability, mobile nodes can get service across domains.

eli5.summary: A travelling phone shows its pass to a gatekeeper that checks who it is and counts how much it uses, even when it is far from home.

questions: what is the diameter mobile ipv4 application
how does aaa work for mobile ip
what is a home agent in mobile ipv4
how are mobile ip session keys distributed
subtitle: How Diameter servers authenticate, authorize and account for Mobile IPv4 users, and hand out the keys they need, even in a foreign network.

tldr.problem: A Mobile IPv4 node that visits a foreign network needs to be authenticated and authorized there, and its home network needs usage records. Doing that with pre-configured keys between every node and every agent does not scale.
tldr.mechanism: The Foreign Agent and Home Agent act as Diameter clients. They send AA-Mobile-Node-Request and Home-Agent-MIP-Request commands to AAA servers. The home AAA server (AAAH) authenticates the mobile node, optionally picks or allocates a Home Agent, and generates session keys and nonces for the three security associations.
tldr.outcome: Mobile nodes can get service from foreign providers without pre-existing relationships with each agent. The application does not apply to Mobile IPv6.

today: RFC 4004 is a Proposed Standard, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It builds on the Diameter base protocol and Mobile IPv4.

sections.title: Why Mobile IPv4 Needs AAA
sections.content:
Mobile IPv4 lets a Mobile Node (MN) change its point of attachment while keeping a fixed home address. A Home Agent (HA) intercepts packets sent to that address and tunnels them to the node. A Foreign Agent (FA) may sit at the visited network and must authenticate each node and verify it may use resources there. It must also report resource use to the home domain.

This RFC defines a Diameter application that meets these Authentication, Authorization and Accounting (AAA) needs. Both the HA and the FA act as Diameter clients. Mobile nodes use only Mobile IPv4 and do not implement Diameter. The visited domain has a foreign AAA server (AAAF), and the home domain has a home AAA server (AAAH).

The application is not applicable to Mobile IPv6.
sections.eli5: A traveller needs the hotel to check their ID and tell their home bank how much they spent. This is the system that lets the hotel and the bank talk.

sections.title: Mobility Security Associations
sections.content:
Mobile IPv4 uses Mobility Security Associations (MSAs): an agreement on a 32-bit Security Parameters Index (SPI), a keyed-hash algorithm and a shared secret. There is an MN-HA MSA, which authenticates Registration Requests (without that protection an attacker could redirect packets anywhere), an optional MN-FA MSA and an optional FA-HA MSA.

Setting these up by hand does not scale to visits in foreign domains. With this application, the MN starts with only a long-term security association with the AAAH, indexed by its Network Access Identifier (NAI). The AAAH authenticates the Registration Request and then generates and distributes MSAs to the MN, HA and FA.

MSAs are unidirectional, so each direction may have different SPIs. This application supports different SPIs per direction but distributes only a single session key for each pair of MSAs between two nodes.
sections.eli5: Each pair of players needs a secret handshake. Instead of everyone memorizing handshakes with everyone, the home office invents them on the spot and passes them out.

sections.title: Message Flows and Home Agent Allocation
sections.content:
When a mobile node sends a Registration Request, the FA builds an AA-Mobile-Node-Request (AMR) and sends it to its AAAF. The AAAF forwards it toward the AAAH, which authenticates the node. The AAAH then sends a Home-Agent-MIP-Request (HAR) to the Home Agent, which answers with a Home-Agent-MIP-Answer (HAA). The AAAH returns an AA-Mobile-Node-Answer (AMA), and the FA sends the Registration Reply to the node. The FA does not need AAA on every Registration Request, only when the prior authorization expires.

The HA can be fixed, allocated in the home realm, or allocated in the foreign network. If the node's home agent field is 0.0.0.0 or 255.255.255.255, the FA sets the Home-Agent-Requested flag. With 255.255.255.255 it also sets the flag that the HA may be allocated only in the home realm. The AAAF may offer an HA in its own domain with the Foreign-Home-Agent-Available flag, and the AAAH decides under local policy.

With a co-located care-of address, no FA is involved. The HA sends the AMR itself, with the Co-Located-Mobile-Node bit set.

Sending keys through intermediate Diameter agents exposes them. If that is a concern, the FA or HA can use a Diameter redirect agent and then set up a TLS or IPSec security association directly with the AAAH. If the AAAH cannot set one up, it returns DIAMETER_ERROR_END_TO_END_MIP_KEY_ENCRYPTION.
sections.eli5: The visited place asks its own office, which asks your home office, which picks a helper at home or abroad and tells everyone it is fine.

sections.title: Commands, AVPs and Result Codes
sections.content:
The application defines two command pairs: AMR/AMA with Command-Code 260 and HAR/HAA with Command-Code 262. Application-Id 2 MUST be used in all AMR/AMA, HAR/HAA and accounting commands. Value 0 SHOULD be used for session termination and abort commands, which the base protocol defines. Diameter RAR/RAA re-authentication commands MUST NOT be sent, because only the mobile node can start re-authentication.

Key AVPs include MIP-Reg-Request (320) and MIP-Reg-Reply (321), which carry the Mobile IPv4 registration messages; MIP-Mobile-Node-Address (333); MIP-Home-Agent-Address (334); and MIP-Feature-Vector (337), a set of flags the FA and AAAF use to request features such as key generation or an HA in a foreign network. MIP-MN-AAA-Auth (322) carries data that helps the AAAH validate the node's authenticator.

Six new result codes are defined: 4005 to 4008 for transient failures and 5024 and 5025 for permanent failures.
sections.eli5: The messages are forms with boxes to fill in. Each box has a number so everyone knows which fact goes where.

sections.title: Key Distribution
sections.content:
After authenticating the node, the AAAH generates three session keys: K1 for MN-HA, K2 for MN-FA and K3 for FA-HA. The keys for the HA and FA travel in Diameter AVPs. The mobile node does not speak Diameter, so it instead receives nonces in the Mobile IPv4 Registration Reply. It combines each nonce with its long-term secret shared with the AAAH to derive the same key.

The AAAH MUST return keys and nonces if they were requested. The nonce MUST be a random value of at least 128 bits, and the FA-HA key is also a random value of at least 128 bits. The algorithm defined is HMAC-SHA-1, value 2.

Two lifetimes apply. The Authorization-Lifetime is the number of seconds before the node must register again. The MIP-MSA-Lifetime is the number of seconds before session keys expire; zero means no timeout, and any non-zero value MUST be at least the Authorization-Lifetime. SPIs for the MSAs MUST NOT fall between 0 and 255, which is reserved.

Once keys are in place, later registrations need not involve the AAA infrastructure until the keys expire.
sections.eli5: The home office makes up secret codes and gives each helper their copy. Your phone only gets a clue, which it mixes with a password it already has to build the same code.

sections.title: Sessions, Handoff and Accounting
sections.content:
The FA picks a session identifier for the AMR, and the AAAH MUST use a different one for the HAR. This lets the FA and HA state be managed independently. When a node moves between foreign agents, the home realm should not see separate sessions, since that could affect billing. The HA creates an Acct-Multi-Session-Id when it is first allocated and MUST return the same value in every HAA, so accounting records correlate across handoffs.

To reach the same AAAH and HA on re-registration, the node SHOULD include the AAAH NAI and HA NAI where it supports the AAA NAI extension.

Mobility agents MUST send a Session-Termination-Request if the Authorization Lifetime has expired and no new registration arrived. The AAAH SHOULD free all resources only after the STR from the home agent, so an STR from one FA does not release home-agent session state. Accounting AVPs such as input and output octets and packets MUST be in all Accounting-Request messages.
sections.eli5: Even if you move between hotels, your home office keeps one running tab for the whole trip.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Where untrusted Diameter agents are present, end-to-end security MUST be used: TLS or IPSec between the AAAH and the FA, and between the AAAH and the HA. The identities in the certificates must be authorized and bound to the Mobile IPv4 Diameter session before the AAAH starts to distribute keys.

Using one session key for both directions of an MSA pair is described as safe here, because the keys only compute keyed hashes that protect the integrity of control messages, Mobile IP has its own replay protection, and requests always differ from responses.

Nonces and authentication extensions can be seen by anyone with a clear copy of the Registration Reply. To resist an offline dictionary attack, the pre-shared key between the node and the AAAH SHOULD be a random value of at least 96 bits. The nonce SHOULD be unique, a random value of at least 128 bits is strongly recommended, and the long-term secret MUST be refreshed periodically by out-of-band means. Setting MIP-MSA-Lifetime to zero is not recommended.
sections.eli5: Pass the secrets through a locked tunnel, make them long and random, and change the main password once in a while.
